slides.title: Vector Space Model
slides.notes: Open by naming the restraint that makes the chapter useful: every object on the slide is a direction through a chosen origin. That restriction is not a weakness. It gives a clean algebra for angles, subspaces, rotations, symmetry groups, and ray observations before later models add structural locations.

slides.title: Directions Before Locations
slides.notes: Use the two drawings to separate representation from interpretation. The same ordered triple can be a direction, a displacement, a velocity, or a temporary coordinate for a point, but the vector-space model only knows the direction algebra. Emphasize that later models will remove this bookkeeping burden.

slides.title: Blades Are Subspaces
slides.notes: Treat blades as weighted oriented subspaces, not as decorative parallelograms. A vector is a one-direction blade, a bivector records an oriented plane element, and a trivector records volume orientation. The dual picture is important because a subspace can also be represented by its orthogonal complement.

slides.title: Direction Product
slides.notes: This is the computational heart of the first half of the chapter. The scalar part of a product measures metric overlap, while the bivector part measures oriented sweep. Keeping both parts together prevents angle computations from losing the plane and orientation in which the angle lives.

slides.title: Planar Triangle
slides.notes: Present the triangle as a closed sum of three direction vectors, then show what happens when the same equality is wedged with each side. The classical sine law appears, but the blade equation is stronger because it still remembers the oriented plane and area element.

slides.title: Projection And Orthogonality
slides.notes: The chapter summary stresses that orthogonal projection of k-directions is well defined by contraction. Use the picture to make that algebraic: a vector splits into an in-plane part and an orthogonal rejection. The bivector plane is a subspace with a metric, not merely a shaded patch.

slides.title: Three Angular Ratios
slides.notes: Move carefully through the three direction pairs. Vector-vector and bivector-bivector angles are both rotor ratios after dualizing the planes. Vector-plane angle is subtler because the perpendicular in-plane direction must be recovered. The point is to keep the full bivector angle instead of extracting only scalars.

slides.title: Spherical Triangle
slides.notes: A spherical triangle is a triangle of directions on the unit sphere. Its vertices are unit vectors, its sides are bivector plane rotations, and its internal angles compare those side planes. The scalar cosine laws can be read from products, but the rotor and bivector data are the real geometry.

slides.title: Rotor From Plane And Angle
slides.notes: A rotor is the even operator that rotates directions by sandwiching. When the rotation plane and angle are known, the formula is immediate, but the slide should stress the half-angle and orientation. The plane-angle product is the geometric quantity; changing orientation changes the sign convention consistently.

slides.title: Rotor From Direction Data
slides.notes: The chapter gives several construction patterns. One unit direction and its image determine the smallest-turn rotor except at the antipodal case. A full frame determines a unique rotor, and many noisy direction pairs ask for a best-fit rotor. The slide links exact algebra to estimation practice.

slides.title: Logarithm And Interpolation
slides.notes: Interpolation should stay on the rotation group. Instead of averaging matrices or Euler angles, take the relative rotor, compute its logarithm, scale the bivector, exponentiate, and apply the partial rotation. The sampled frames show that every intermediate state remains orthogonal and length preserving.

slides.title: Point Groups
slides.notes: Crystallography is a natural vector-space-model application because the symmetry is local around a fixed point. Reflections use unit normal vectors as versors, and even products generate rotations. The cube orbit gives a finite, inspectable example of equivalent directions produced by repeated sandwiching operations.

slides.title: Camera Rays
slides.notes: External camera calibration is the chapter's cautionary application. Image measurements become ray directions after internal calibration, but camera centers and world markers are locations. The vector-space model can still support the computation if names, depths, translations, and ray directions are kept in separate algebraic roles.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close by making the model choice explicit. If the problem is angular, rotational, or fixed-point symmetric, the vector-space model is usually the cleanest algebra. If incidence among offset points, lines, planes, spheres, or translations becomes structural, the course is ready to move to homogeneous and conformal models.
